title: Chapter 19. Of the Several Kinds of Commonwealth by Institution, and of Succession to the Sovereign Power
paragraphs: The difference between commonwealths consists in the difference of the sovereign, or person representing all and every one of the multitude. And since the sovereignty is either in one man, or in an assembly of more than one — and into that assembly either every man has the right to enter, or not every one but certain men set apart from the rest — it is plain that there can be only three kinds of commonwealth. For the representative must be either one man or more; and if more, then either an assembly of all, or only of a part. When the representative is one man, the commonwealth is a MONARCHY. When it is an assembly of all who choose to come together, it is a DEMOCRACY, or popular commonwealth. When it is an assembly of only a part, it is called an ARISTOCRACY. No other kind of commonwealth is possible: for either one, or more, or all must have the sovereign power (which I have shown to be indivisible) entire.

There are other names for forms of government in the histories and in books of politics — tyranny and oligarchy. But these are not names of other forms of government; they are names of the same forms, disliked. Those who are unhappy under a monarchy call it tyranny; those displeased with an aristocracy call it oligarchy; and likewise those who feel aggrieved under a democracy call it anarchy (which means absence of government) — though I think no one believes that absence of government is itself a new kind of government. By the same reasoning, men ought not to believe that the government is one kind when they like it and another when they dislike it or are oppressed by the governors.

It is plain that men who are at absolute liberty may, if they choose, give authority to one man to represent every one of them, just as they may give such authority to any assembly of men whatever; and so they may submit themselves, if they think fit, to a monarch as absolutely as to any other representative. So where a sovereign power has already been erected, no other representative of the same people can exist, except for certain particular ends, limited by the sovereign. To do otherwise would be to erect two sovereigns, and to have every man's person represented by two actors who, by opposing each other, would necessarily divide that power which (if men wish to live in peace) is indivisible, and so reduce the multitude to the condition of war — contrary to the end for which all sovereignty is instituted. And so, just as it is absurd to think that a sovereign assembly inviting the people of its dominion to send up their deputies, with power to make known their advice or wishes, should on that account hold those deputies, rather than itself, to be the absolute representative of the people, so it is absurd to think the same in a monarchy. I do not know how this so plain a truth has of late been so little observed: that in a monarchy, the man who had the sovereignty by 600 years of descent, alone called sovereign, given the title of Majesty by every one of his subjects, and unquestionably taken by them for their king, was nevertheless not considered as their representative; the name passing without contradiction to those men who, at his command, were sent up by the people to carry their petitions, and to offer him (if he permitted) their advice. This may serve as a warning to those who are the true and absolute representative of a people: to instruct men in the nature of that office, and to take care how they admit of any other general representation, on any occasion whatever, if they mean to discharge the trust committed to them.

The difference between these three kinds of commonwealth does not lie in any difference of power but in their convenience, or fitness, for producing the peace and security of the people — the end for which they were instituted. To compare monarchy with the other two, we should observe, first, that whoever bears the person of the people, or is one of the assembly that bears it, also bears his own natural person. And though in his political person he is careful to procure the common interest, he is no less — or even more — careful to procure the private good of himself, his family, his kindred, and his friends; and for the most part, if the public interest happens to clash with the private, he prefers the private. For men's passions are commonly more powerful than their reason. From this it follows that where the public and private interest are most closely united, there the public is most advanced. Now in a monarchy, the private interest is the same as the public. The riches, power, and honour of a monarch arise only from the riches, strength, and reputation of his subjects. For no king can be rich, glorious, or secure whose subjects are poor, contemptible, or too weak — through want, or through dissension — to maintain a war against their enemies. Whereas in a democracy or aristocracy, public prosperity does not contribute to the private fortune of a corrupt or ambitious man so much as does a treacherous piece of advice, a treacherous action, or a civil war.

Second, a monarch receives counsel from whomever, whenever, and wherever he pleases; and so may hear the opinions of men versed in the matter he is deliberating on, of whatever rank or quality, as long before the time of action and with as much secrecy as he wishes. But when a sovereign assembly needs counsel, none are admitted except those who have a right of admission from the start; and most of those have been versed more in the acquisition of wealth than of knowledge, and must give their advice in long speeches — which may, and commonly do, stir men to action, but do not govern them in it. For the understanding is never enlightened by the flame of the passions, but dazzled. Nor is there any place or time in which an assembly can receive counsel in secret, because of its own size.

Third, the resolutions of a monarch are subject to no inconstancy other than that of human nature. But in assemblies, besides the inconstancy of nature, there arises an inconstancy from the sheer number. The absence of a few who would have kept a resolution, once taken, firm (which may happen through complacency, negligence, or private hindrance), or the diligent appearance of a few of the opposite opinion, undoes today everything that was concluded yesterday.
Fourth, a monarch cannot disagree with himself out of envy or interest, but an assembly can — and to such a degree that it may produce a civil war.

Fifth, in monarchy there is this inconvenience: that any subject, by the power of one man, for the enriching of a favourite or flatterer, may be deprived of all he owns; which I admit is a great and unavoidable inconvenience. But the same may happen where the sovereign power is in an assembly: their power is the same; and they are as liable to evil counsel, and to being seduced by orators, as a monarch is by flatterers, and they become each other's flatterers, serving one another's covetousness and ambition in turn. And whereas the favourites of an assembly are many, and the kindred far more numerous, than those of any monarch — besides, there is no favourite of a monarch who cannot equally help his friends as harm his enemies, while orators (that is, favourites of sovereign assemblies), though they have great power to harm, have little to save. For to accuse takes less eloquence (such is man's nature) than to excuse; and condemnation more closely resembles justice than absolution does.

Sixth, it is an inconvenience in monarchy that the sovereignty may descend on an infant, or on one who cannot tell good from evil — the difficulty being that the use of his power must then be in the hand of another man, or of some assembly of men, who are to govern by his right and in his name, as guardians and protectors of his person and authority. But to say it is inconvenient to put the use of sovereign power into the hand of a man, or an assembly, is to say that all government is more inconvenient than confusion and civil war. And so all the danger that can be alleged must come from the contention of those who, for an office of such great honour and profit, may become competitors. To show that this inconvenience does not arise from the form of government we call monarchy, we should consider that the previous monarch has appointed who shall have the tutelage of his infant successor — either expressly by testament, or tacitly by not opposing the custom received in such cases. If there is then any inconvenience, it is to be attributed not to the monarchy but to the ambition and injustice of subjects; which, in every kind of government where the people are not well instructed in their duty and in the rights of sovereignty, is the same. Or else the previous monarch has made no provision at all for such tutelage; and then the law of nature has supplied this sufficient rule: that the tutelage shall be in him who by nature has the greatest interest in preserving the authority of the infant, and to whom the least benefit can come from his death or diminishment. For since every man by nature seeks his own benefit and advancement, to put an infant into the power of those who can promote themselves by his destruction or damage is not guardianship but treachery. So with sufficient provision taken against any just quarrel about the government under a child, if any contention arises that disturbs the public peace, it is not to be attributed to the form of monarchy but to the ambition of subjects and their ignorance of their duty. On the other side, there is no great commonwealth whose sovereignty is in a great assembly that is not, in matters of consultation about peace and war, and in making laws, in the same condition as if the government were in a child. For as a child lacks the judgement to dissent from counsel given him, and so is forced to take the advice of those, or of him, to whom he is committed, so an assembly lacks the liberty to dissent from the counsel of the majority, good or bad. And as a child needs a tutor or protector to preserve his person and authority, so also (in great commonwealths) the sovereign assembly, in all great dangers and troubles, has need of custodes libertatis — that is, of dictators, or protectors of their authority — which are in effect temporary monarchs, to whom for a time they may commit the entire exercise of their power; and these have, at the end of that time, been deprived of it more often than infant kings have been deprived by their protectors, regents, or other tutors.

Though the kinds of sovereignty are, as I have now shown, only three — monarchy, where one man has it; democracy, where the general assembly of subjects has it; or aristocracy, where it is in an assembly of certain persons nominated, or otherwise marked out from the rest — yet anyone who considers the particular commonwealths that have existed, and that exist, in the world may not easily reduce them to three, and may be inclined to think there are other forms, arising from these mixed together. For example: elective kingdoms, where kings have the sovereign power put into their hands for a time; or kingdoms in which the king has a limited power. Such governments are nevertheless called monarchies by most writers. Likewise, if a popular or aristocratic commonwealth subdues an enemy's country and governs it by a president, procurator, or other magistrate, this may at first sight seem to be a democratic or aristocratic government. But it is not. For elective kings are not sovereigns but ministers of the sovereign; nor are limited kings sovereigns, but ministers of those who hold the sovereign power; nor are provinces subject to a democracy or aristocracy of another commonwealth governed democratically or aristocratically, but monarchically.

And first, concerning an elective king whose power is limited to his life, as it is in many parts of Christendom today, or to a certain number of years or months, as the Dictator's power was at Rome: if he has the right to appoint his successor, he is no longer elective but hereditary. But if he has no power to elect his successor, then there must be some other man, or known assembly, that may after his death elect a new one — or else the commonwealth dies and dissolves with him, and returns to the condition of war. If it is known who have the power to give the sovereignty after his death, it is known also that the sovereignty was in them before; for no one has the right to give what he has no right to possess and to keep to himself, if he thinks fit. But if there is no one who can give the sovereignty after the death of the first elected, then he himself has the power — indeed he is obliged by the law of nature — to provide, by appointing his successor, against the people who trusted him with the government slipping back into the miserable condition of civil war. And consequently he was, when elected, an absolute sovereign.

Second: a king whose power is limited is not superior to him, or to them, who have the power to limit it; and one who is not superior is not supreme — that is, not sovereign. The sovereignty therefore was always in that assembly which had the right to limit him; and so the government was not monarchy but either democracy or aristocracy. So it was in ancient Sparta, where the kings had the privilege of leading their armies but the sovereignty was in the Ephors.

Third, whereas in former times the Roman people governed (for example) the land of Judea by a president, Judea was not therefore a democracy, because the Jews were not governed by any assembly which any of them had the right to enter; nor was it an aristocracy, because they were not governed by any assembly which any man could enter by their election. They were governed by one person, who though to the people of Rome was an assembly of the people, or democracy, was as far as the people of Judea were concerned — who had no right at all to participate in the government — a monarch. For though where the people are governed by an assembly chosen by themselves out of their own number, the government is called democracy or aristocracy, when they are governed by an assembly not of their own choosing, it is a monarchy: not of one man over another man, but of one people over another people.

In every one of these forms of government, the matter being mortal — so that not only monarchs but whole assemblies die — it is necessary for preserving the peace among men that, just as order was taken for an artificial man, so also order should be taken for an artificial eternity of life. Without that, men who are governed by an assembly would return into the condition of war in every age, and those who are governed by one man as soon as their governor dies. This artificial eternity is what men call the right of succession.

No form of government is perfect where the disposing of the succession is not in the present sovereign. For if it is in any other particular man, or in any private assembly, it is in a person who is a subject, and may be assumed by the sovereign at his pleasure — and so the right is in himself. And if it is in no particular man, but left to a new choice, then the commonwealth is dissolved, and the right is in whoever can seize it; contrary to the intention of those who instituted the commonwealth for their perpetual, not temporary, security.
In a democracy, the whole assembly cannot fail unless the multitude that is to be governed fails. And so questions of the right of succession have no place at all in that form of government.

In an aristocracy, when any member of the assembly dies, the election of another to fill his place belongs to the assembly, as the sovereign — to whom belongs the choosing of all counsellors and officers. For what the representative does as actor, every one of the subjects does as author. And though the sovereign assembly may give power to others to elect new men to fill its ranks, the election is still made by its authority; and by the same authority it may, when the public requires, be recalled.

The present monarch has the right to dispose of the succession. The greatest difficulty about the right of succession is in monarchy; and the difficulty arises from this: that at first sight it is not clear who is to appoint the successor, nor often who it is whom he has appointed. For in both these matters a more exact reasoning is needed than every man is used to. As for the question of who shall appoint the successor of a monarch holding sovereign authority (that is — for elective kings and princes do not hold the sovereign power as property but only in use), we must consider that either the man in possession has the right to dispose of the succession, or that right is once again in the dissolved multitude. For the death of him who holds the sovereign power as his property leaves the multitude without any sovereign at all — that is, without any representative in whom they may be united and capable of doing any single action. They are therefore incapable of electing a new monarch; every man having equal right to submit himself to whoever he thinks best able to protect him, or if he can, to protect himself by his own sword. Which is a return to confusion and to the condition of a war of every man against every man, contrary to the end for which monarchy had its first institution. So it is plain that by the institution of monarchy, the disposing of the successor is always left to the judgement and will of the present possessor.

And as for the question (which may sometimes arise) of who it is that the monarch in possession has designated for the succession and inheritance of his power, this is settled by his express words and testament, or by other tacit signs that are sufficient.

By express words, or by testament, when he declares it in his lifetime, viva voce or in writing — as the first emperors of Rome declared who should be their heirs. For the word 'heir' does not in itself imply the children, or nearest kindred, of a man; it means whoever a man shall in any way declare he wishes to succeed him in his estate. If therefore a monarch expressly declares, by word or in writing, that such a man shall be his heir, then that man is immediately on the death of his predecessor invested in the right of being monarch.

But where testament and express words are wanting, other natural signs of his will are to be followed; one of which is custom. So where the custom is that the next of kin succeeds absolutely, there also the next of kin has the right to the succession; because if the will of the man who was in possession had been otherwise, he could easily have declared the same in his lifetime. And likewise where the custom is that the next of the male kindred succeeds, there too the right of succession is in the next male kinsman, for the same reason. And so it is also if the custom were to advance the female. For whatever custom a man may by a word override, and does not, is a natural sign that he would have the custom stand.

But where neither custom nor testament has gone before, it is to be understood, first, that a monarch's will is that the government remain monarchical, because he has approved that form of government in himself. Second, that a child of his own, male or female, is to be preferred to any other; because men are presumed to be more inclined by nature to advance their own children than the children of other men — and, of their own, rather a male than a female, because men are naturally fitter than women for actions of labour and danger. Third, where his own issue fails, a brother is preferred over a stranger, and the closer in blood over the more remote; because it is always presumed that the nearer of kin is the nearer in affection. And it is evident that a man always receives, by reflection, the most honour from the greatness of his closest kin.

But if it is lawful for a monarch to dispose of the succession by words of contract or by testament, men may perhaps object a great inconvenience: that he may sell, or give, his right of governing to a stranger; which, because strangers (that is, men not used to living under the same government, not speaking the same language) commonly undervalue one another, may turn to the oppression of his subjects. This is indeed a great inconvenience; but it does not necessarily follow from subjection to a stranger's government, but from the unskillfulness of the governors, ignorant of the true rules of politics. And so the Romans, when they had subdued many nations, in order to make their government digestible, used to remove that grievance as far as they thought necessary by giving, sometimes to whole nations, and sometimes to the principal men of every nation they conquered, not only the privileges but also the name of Romans, and by taking many of them into the Senate and into offices of charge, even in the city of Rome itself. This was what our most wise king, King James, aimed at in seeking the union of his two realms of England and Scotland. If he could have achieved it, in all likelihood it would have prevented the civil wars that make both those kingdoms now miserable. So it is no injury to the people for a monarch to dispose of the succession by will, though by the fault of many princes it has sometimes proved inconvenient. As another argument for its lawfulness: whatever inconvenience may come from giving a kingdom to a stranger may also come from marrying so with strangers that the right of succession may descend to them — yet this is by everyone accounted lawful.
